name: UCC24612-1DBVR
title: High-frequency synchronous rectifier controller, SOT-23-5
summary: A secondary-side synchronous rectifier controller that drives an external N-channel MOSFET in place of an output diode, deciding when to conduct from the MOSFET's own drain-to-source voltage. It senses drains up to 230 V, runs from a VDD of 4 V to 28 V through an internal 9.5 V regulator that also clamps the gate drive, and drives with 1 A source and 4 A sink plus proportional gate drive for clean CCM turn-off. Adaptive off-time blanking and frequency-based standby (320 µA typical at 5 V) need no programming pins. Two variants differ in turn-on delay and minimum on-time: UCC24612-1 to 1 MHz and UCC24612-2 to 800 kHz.
key_figures: 1 A source, 4 A sink, clamped at 9.5 V
320 µA typ at VDD = 5 V; 390 µA at 12 V

pins.name: VG
pins.function: SR MOSFET gate drive. A small series resistor and short tracks join it to the gate. Into a large N-channel MOSFET the peak current exceeds 1 A when sourcing (high) and 4 A when sinking (low). The pull-up turns weak once the fast initial rise is over, so a resistance below 50 kΩ from VG to VS must be avoided.

pins.name: VS
pins.function: Chip ground reference, and the source-side sense input for the drop across the SR MOSFET. Its track runs separately from the power path so parasitic inductance does not enter the sensed voltage.

pins.name: REG
pins.function: Bias rail of the chip: output of the internal linear regulator from VDD, held at 9.5 V. A 2.2 µF capacitor between REG and VS decouples it.

pins.name: VDD
pins.function: Input of the internal linear regulator. In the low-side configuration connect it to the output voltage; in the high-side configuration derive it from the SR drain with an R-C-D network or another bias circuit.

pins.name: VD
pins.function: Drain voltage sense. Connect to the SR MOSFET drain with a trace that does not share the power path, so parasitic inductance does not distort the sensed voltage.

circuits.title: Flyback with low-side SR, VDD from the output
circuits.description: The rectifier MOSFET Q1 sits in the return leg of the flyback secondary, its source on the output ground. VD and VS sense Q1's drain and source; VG drives its gate directly. VDD is fed straight from the output rail, and CREG decouples the 9.5 V REG supply to VS.

parts.note: flyback transformer; P1 primary dot end, P2 primary other end, S1 secondary dot end, S2 secondary other end
synchronous rectifier MOSFET, body diode also drawn beside it

circuits.title: Low-side SR biased from the drain for a low output voltage
circuits.description: A low-side SR as in the basic connection, but VDD is not taken from the output: D1 and R1 feed CVDD and VDD from the SR drain, so the controller keeps its supply when an overloaded 5 V output drops too low to turn the SR on. The drain-fed bias copes with a wide voltage range but is far less efficient than an auxiliary winding.

parts.note: flyback transformer; P1 primary dot end, P2 primary other end, S1 secondary dot end, S2 secondary other end
synchronous rectifier MOSFET, body diode also drawn beside it

circuits.title: Flyback with high-side SR, VDD from a diode and R-C filter
circuits.description: Q1 sits in the positive leg: its source and the controller's VS ride on the switching end of the secondary, its drain is the output. VDD is made relative to VS by D1 from the drain (the output rail) through R1 into CVDD. This is the simple, low-cost high-side bias; VD varies widely (reflected input plus output voltage), so in some designs the VDD it gives can exceed the VDD rating.

synchronous rectifier MOSFET, body diode also drawn beside it

circuits.title: High-side SR powered from an auxiliary winding
circuits.description: A high-side SR whose supply comes from an extra secondary winding referred to the SR source: D1 rectifies it into CVDD, and through the transformer coupling VDD is in effect the output voltage. It is the most efficient bias choice, limited by transformer construction and cost.

parts.note: flyback transformer with secondary-side auxiliary winding; P1/P2 primary (P1 dot), S1/S2 secondary (S1 dot), A1/A2 auxiliary (A1 dot)
synchronous rectifier MOSFET, body diode also drawn beside it

circuits.title: High-side SR powered through a depletion-mode MOSFET
circuits.description: D1 takes power from the SR drain as in the R-C-D bias, and a depletion-mode MOSFET Q3, its gate on REG, passes it on to VDD. VDD stays well regulated over the whole operating range without a transformer change, though drawing bias from the high drain voltage still costs efficiency.

circuits.title: Evaluation module as the low-side rectifier of a 20 V, 60 W DCM flyback
circuits.description: The UCC24612 evaluation board replaces the output diode of an offline 20 V, 60 W DCM flyback run by a UCC28740 primary controller at up to 85 kHz. J1 drops into the diode's place in the secondary return: pin 1 to the winding (SR drain, TP2), pin 2 to output ground (SR source, TP1). U1 drives Q1 through R1; C1 decouples REG and C2 decouples VDD, both to VS. With JP1 closed, VDD comes from the output (TP3) through R4; with JP1 open it comes from TP3 through D2 and R2 instead. A 27 V zener D1 sits from VDD to VS. R3 and C3 are an optional R-C snubber across Q1.

operation.text: UCC24612-1 has an 80 ns typical turn-on delay, 375 ns minimum on-time and runs up to 1 MHz; it suits standard flybacks and active-clamp flybacks with GaN primary switches. UCC24612-2 has 170 ns and 540 ns and runs up to 800 kHz; the longer delay rides out the leading current spike seen with silicon super-junction primary switches in active-clamp flybacks, and the longer on-time suits the resonant current shape of LLC converters.

The controller watches the SR MOSFET's drain-to-source voltage between VD and VS. VG goes high when VDS drops below VTHVGON (about -240 mV) and low when VDS rises back above VTHVGOFF (about -9 mV). Because the conducting SR sees a negative VDS, a larger negative drop means more current. During the turn-on delay the body diode carries the current, which in a flyback is then at its peak.

All internal circuits run from REG, which an internal linear regulator makes from VDD. With VDD above 9.5 V, REG is regulated at 9.5 V, which also sets the gate drive level; the regulator supports 10 mA average load. Below 9.5 V the regulator passes VDD through with roughly 0.2 V drop, depending on load. The regulator needs enough REG capacitance to be stable; 2.2 µF is the recommended value.

UVLO watches REG, not VDD. Below VREGON at start-up, or after REG falls under VREGOFF, the chip draws only IVDDSTART (typically under 120 µA) and most functions are off. Above 2 V on REG, VG is actively pulled to VS; below 2 V a weaker pull-down remains. Once REG passes VREGON the chip draws full current and starts driving the SR.

As the SR current falls toward zero and VDS reaches -50 mV, the controller lowers the gate voltage to hold VDS near -50 mV instead of keeping the gate fully on. This avoids turning off too soon, which would cost diode conduction and recovery loss, and shortens the turn-off delay because the gate is already near threshold when the turn-off comparator trips. In CCM flybacks the turn-off di/dt can reach 150 A/µs, so the shorter delay reduces negative current.

operation.topic: Forced proportional drive in deep CCM
operation.text: Where the SR current at turn-off is still large and VDS never reaches -50 mV (for example low-voltage telecom bricks run in deep CCM), the controller moves the threshold to -150 mV near the end of the conduction interval, timed from the previous cycle's conduction time, so the gate is pulled down early for a fast turn-off. -150 mV is the deepest level available, so the SR MOSFET must let VDS reach it at the deep-CCM turn-off current. Normal proportional drive and turn-off stay active, so a conduction time that changes greatly within two cycles is still handled.

operation.topic: Proportional drive held off in the first half
operation.text: In LLC and active-clamp flybacks the SR current rises before it falls. To keep proportional drive from engaging at the start, it stays off until half of the previous cycle's conduction time has passed, so it acts only on the falling slope.

Right after turn-on the turn-off comparator is blanked for the fixed tON(min), so ringing from the MOSFET package inductance cannot trip it; the SR conducts at least that long whatever the comparator says. The blanking is short enough for 1 MHz (UCC24612-1) or 800 kHz (UCC24612-2) operation. Snubbing and low-inductance MOSFET packages reduce the ringing further.

After turn-off, a DCM ring can swing the drain below the turn-on threshold. The turn-on comparator is blanked for the largest of three times: the absolute minimum tOFF_ABSMIN, a clamp set by the recorded DCM ring period, and 70 % of the SR off time measured in the cycle before. No programming pin is needed.

If the SR turns on again after an insufficient blanking time, the false conduction ends at the minimum on-time. A conduction no longer than the minimum on-time is taken as a ring-triggered false turn-on; the time from the previous turn-off to it is stored as the ring period, and from the next cycle the blanking clamp becomes 2.2 times that period.

If the body diode conducts during the blanking time for longer than the minimum on-time, the clamp is too long (for example a QR converter at high line) and is reset to the absolute minimum. If blanking ends after body-diode conduction has begun, turn-on is skipped for that cycle, since a forced minimum on-time late in a CCM cycle could cause shoot-through. The off-blanking time is limited to tOFF_MAX, 3.68 µs typical.
VG can turn on only once the controller is armed for the cycle, which happens when TOFFBLANK expires; that timer starts only after VD rises 500 mV above VS.

The gate driver runs from REG, so the gate is clamped at 9.5 V however high VDD is, for fast switching and low drive loss; the 9.5 V level is set for low conduction loss in non-logic-level MOSFETs. When VDD is near or under 9.5 V, REG follows VDD less VREGDO and the gate drive is correspondingly lower but still works; the chip stops when REG drops below UVLO.

Standby is decided by average SR switching frequency, not conduction time. Below 12 kHz average the controller enters standby, holds VG low and draws IVDDSTBY, while still monitoring switching, REG and keeping the gate pull-down active. When the average frequency exceeds 15 kHz over a 4.5 ms window, SR operation resumes, ignoring the first six switching cycles so the SR is not turned on mid-cycle.

Outside UVLO and standby all control and timing functions run. REG current is IVDDRUN plus the average gate charge current of the SR MOSFET, and the gate voltage follows VDS through proportional drive.

REG needs at least 1.5 µF, and at least 2.2 µF once the average gate charge current exceeds 5 mA. VDD should stay between 4.5 V and 28 V. In low-side use VDD can connect straight to an output of 4.5 V to 28 V. In high-side use there are three options: a secondary-side auxiliary winding (best efficiency, constrained by transformer design), a diode and R-C filter from the drain (simplest and cheapest, but the drain swing can push VDD past its rating), or a diode from the drain feeding a depletion-mode MOSFET (regulated VDD without changing the transformer, at some efficiency cost). A 5 V low-side design whose output collapses in overload can also use the R-C-D bias to keep the gate driven.

Lower on-resistance cuts conduction loss but reduces light-load efficiency, and proportional drive erodes its benefit. Choose RDS(on) so proportional drive is active for under half of the full-load conduction time. The breakdown voltage must exceed the highest drain stress at maximum input voltage.
A 2.2 µF, 50 V ceramic capacitor decouples REG. VDD usually sits on the output with plenty of capacitance, but a 0.1 µF ceramic close to the chip is still advised for high-frequency current.

To size the R-C snubber across the SR, measure the secondary ring frequency in circuit with the SR not driven (TP3 disconnected from the converter so Q1 stays off) at partial load to limit body-diode heating, and know the secondary leakage inductance. Compute the winding capacitance, then the damping resistor for Q = 1, then the series capacitor from the switching frequency.

Keep current loops and tracks short, especially on single-sided boards. Put ceramic bypass capacitors right at VDD-to-VS and REG-to-VS. Run VD and VS as separate tracks straight to the MOSFET drain and source pads so stray inductance in the power path is not sensed, which would turn the SR off early; the VS track carries both gate return and sense, so keep it short. Run VG and VS as a parallel pair to the MOSFET and add a series gate resistor if ringing needs damping.
ESD protection is limited; store and handle with leads shorted or in conductive foam.
